b: The first artificial intelligence belonged to the Olympian gods. The robotic handmaids of Hephaestus, described in Homer’s Iliad, moved fast and looked like young women. They possessed a capacity for speech and thought surpassing human ability. The history of robotics, as Adrienne Mayor has written, teaches us that “automata fall into three basic functions: labor, sex, and entertainment or spectacle.”1 In Homer, we get three for the price of one. The golden maidens of the forge toil in service to divine craft, and for the titillation of the reader.

Effortless labor is the fantasy at the center of artificial intelligence. But for thousands of years, artificial intelligence has always depended on hidden labor. Classical antiquity reveals the viscerally human costs of outsourcing cognition in pursuit of superhuman power.

And such artificial beings aren’t confined to myth. More prescient, and more unsettling, is the actual history of the ancients making intelligent machines out of human minds. The Roman elite, for example, augmented human intelligence through human labor: specifically, slaves.

Consider Herodes Atticus, a Roman senator who raised a cohort of enslaved children as teaching tools for his own family. Learning that his son could not master the alphabet—an early instance of dyslexia—Herodes conceived the idea “to raise alongside his son 24 slave-boys, of the same age and each named for one of the letters.”2 This was an extraordinary outlay of financial and human capital: 24 enslaved playmates, in a household where Herodes reared only six natural children of his own. More evocative than the expense, however, is the figuration of each slave-boy as a living letter, as a mental prosthetic for the free-born son. Imagine Herodes’s heir in the classroom, arranging these letter-boys in syllables or phonetic clusters, the way that ancient children practiced with pen and papyrus.

These alphabetic brethren were brought into existence exclusively as mnemonics for an elite child. And the moment Herodes’s son grasped their grammatic essence, these boys would be decommissioned as obsolete hardware. Their fate—like their names—was never recorded.

Or consider an exorbitantly rich slaveholder named Calvisius Sabinus. According to the letters of Seneca the Younger, Sabinus collected a library of sorts: a stable of slaves who had committed all the Greek poets to memory. If ever Sabinus desired a book that had not yet been memorized, he placed an order for a new slave “custom-made.” Sabinus assembled this enslaved archive not to edify his intellect but to impress dinner guests. Summoning his slaves for parties, he would command them to deliver just the right verses for himself to repeat.

It would have been cheaper, Sabinus’s friends teased, to buy and learn the books himself. But get real. Who needs to know anything when there’s a computer in your pocket? “What anyone in his household knew,” Sabinus insisted, he himself could be said to know.3

In the age of AI, Bill Gates predicts that “intelligence will be completely free.” … Yet Seneca’s letter points to the darker possibility that effortless intelligence will always rest on someone else’s labor.

Seneca tells the story of Calvisius Sabinus for the same reason that college professors like me tell their students not to rely on ChatGPT. To argue that users of the enslaved archive neither acquire nor internalize the information within. To show that Sabinus exploits artificial intelligence but cultivates no wisdom.

But Seneca also prefigures, with uncanny clarity, the fantasy of possessing encyclopedic knowledge without personal exertion or ethical accountability. The production of human alphabets and enslaved archives was prohibitively expensive in Seneca’s day—feasible only for the ultra-rich, like Herodes Atticus and Sabinus. It’s not hard to imagine how Seneca’s horror would scale at the thought of a world where all of us can command the right verses of Homer to be whispered in our earbuds.

In the age of AI, Bill Gates predicts that “intelligence will be completely free.” Maybe he’s right. Maybe there will come a day with no meaningful barriers to consulting AI. Yet Seneca’s letter points to the darker possibility that effortless intelligence will always rest on someone else’s labor.
Our conundrum is no longer what these large language models (LLMs) can do, but what we are willing to do with them. What will we justify as automation becomes cheap, frictionless, and obedient?
We cannot say that we were not warned.

The poet Hesiod relates how the Greek gods once crafted an artificial woman, “Pandora,” from earth and water. They sculpted her face with immortal beauty and ornamented her with golden jewelry. But deep in her hardware—where none but the gods could see—were installed the “lies and wily words and cunning character”4 of Zeus’s design. This is the terrible irony of the name Pandora—meaning “all-gift”—since each god “gifted” Pandora with a special trait to doom mankind.

Perhaps this version is too dark a telling of Pandora. Too dreary an analogy for the “all-gift” that today’s titans of technology seek to bestow on humanity. A happier rendition might recall that the myth of Pandora began with the titan Prometheus and his pursuit of a better life. The gods, Hesiod claims, had “hidden away” the tools of easy living.5 But Prometheus knew that a spark of Zeus’s fire could supply the human race with a year’s sustenance in a single day. And so Prometheus stole it, lighting a torch with the promise of effortless productivity.

The techno-optimists of 2026 radiate the same expectancy of AI-fueled abundance. “Technology brings incredible benefits, but we must ensure everyone has access to them.” Thus urges Sundar Pichai, CEO of Google, as he proffers a new flame for human flourishing. “We have the opportunity to improve lives at a once-in-a-generation scale.”6 This greed for godlike power, the ache for relief from earthly toil—who can blame Prometheus, really? Who among us has not yearned to play with fire?
Figure 1: Red-figure calyx-krater, c. 450 BC, Attica, Greece, Niobid Painter. British Museum, London.

Artificial intelligence becomes most enticing when its aesthetic appeal feeds the illusion of effortless labor. We can begin to detect this danger in a famous illustration of Pandora from the Niobid Painter, circa 450 BC (fig. 1). There is something disturbing about this Pandora against the black backdrop. She alone of her companions on the krater stands full frontal, arms stiff at her sides and staring out with a look of deadened pleasantry. The painter, like most of Athens’s greatest artists, presents us with a scene just before the climactic moment. Before Pandora descends to earth. Before she seduces the brother of Prometheus. Before she opens her jar and lets loose all the agonies of man. Pandora is, as Hesiod wrote, a kalon kakon—a “beautiful evil”7—whose destructive potential we can sense but cannot stop.

Aesthetics are never just aesthetics. Not in Greek mythology. And not in the technological arms race to design the most seductive intelligent machines. Big tech has long recognized the appeal of consumer-facing virtual assistants with human names and personalities. Compliant female personae predominated in the 2010s, as Microsoft’s Cortana and Amazon’s Alexa joined the conversation that Siri once monopolized.8

Now in the 2020s, users of large language models are seeking oracles more than assistants. Accordingly, Anthropic has crafted “Claude” in honor of the polymathic inventor Claude Shannon, who had himself named his artificially intelligent mouse “Theseus” after the labyrinth-solving demigod. (Interestingly, Shannon appears to have been as reliant on the mathematical brilliance of his wife, Betty, as Theseus was on the maiden Ariadne—but that’s a myth for another day).

And before unveiling the chatbot Gemini, Google had initially christened its generative AI as “Bard”: a term for an epic storyteller that remains closely associated with Homer and Hesiod. Antiquity runs deep in the source code.
Humanity is habituated to reach for divine fire. We spare no art or artifice—concepts that Greek captures in the single word techne—in our determination to attain it.

These are the truths that surely confronted the craftsman Daedalus as he watched his only child fly, and then fall, too close to the sun on the artificial wings. More perilous prosthetics than the letter-boys of Herodes Atticus. How ingenious and dire, these designs by which each generation of fathers tries to propel their sons.

In the Saraceni painting of Icarus, the boy’s fingers swipe at empty air, grasp for loose feathers as mortal gravity pulls on his frame (fig. 2). Even in freefall, he reaches for the fire of the sun. We think we know the lesson, the moral of this story: Man is not meant to fly too far beyond his station.
Figure 2: Caduta di Icaro, 1606–7, Rome, Carlo Saraceni. Museo di Capodimonte, Naples, Italy.

But what of the ecstasy before the fall, when Icarus launches beyond the limits of the earth? The Roman poet Ovid recalls that Icarus had witnesses, a shepherd and a fisherman, who looked up and thought they saw a god. For an instant, they were right. On wings of wood and twine and wax, Icarus momentarily inhabited the heavens.
The glow of the sun blinds us all to the costs of ambition.

The myth and the moral of Icarus are rightly famous. Less well known are the reports of Icarus reenactments in ancient ritual and spectacle. The notorious emperor Nero, for one, enticed Greek youths to reperform shocking moments of their own mythology. One young man assigned to play Icarus tumbled to his death during his first attempt with wings and “spattered the emperor with blood.”9 This story has survived to the present because it illustrates Nero’s menace.

But the irony of the spectacle is that the young performer was never supposed to die. Through some combination of stunt work and a flying harness, this new Icarus was meant to display themythic made possible.

Testing and retesting. The newest iterations of human artifice. And when it comes to the safeguards of emergent technology, as Sam Altman qualified in 2023—before the AI-related deaths of our own young men in Florida, Texas, and California—well … “there will be mistakes.”10

Or maybe these Icaruses are not mistakes. Maybe they are the sacrifices we willingly make in the name of optimization. On the island of Lefkada, the ancient Greeks are said to have sacrificed one criminal each year by fitting him with wings and then launching him from a rocky cliff. The ritual was meant to honor Apollo. But the attachment of wings—even live birds, according to Strabo11—is a curious detail. Why prepare a condemned criminal to fly? Did the Lefkadians dare to dream that one of these improbable Icaruses might remain aloft, proving his favor with the gods and the feasibility of human flight? None, to our knowledge, ever did. Instead, the Lefkadians gathered the bodies of these failed flyers from the waters below. In fishing boats, they rowed the corpses beyond the borders of their island, averting the contamination of the sacrifice. This is classic Greek ritual, of course—purifying the community by eradicating pollution.

And yet—could it be that after every flight and every fall, the Lefkadians could not bear to look upon the remains of another Icarus? Bodies and broken wings sink to the seabed or wash up on foreign shores like the refuse of a botched experiment.

We in modernity make no less use of exploited minds and bodies than our ancient counterparts. We simply make less spectacle. Today’s “letter-boys” labor as data annotators and content moderators in windowless offices across Kenya and Uganda.12 Today’s Icaruses flit through city streets in robotaxis secretly powered by pilots in the Philippines.13 The peculiar artifice of our AI revolution is “a hidden army of workers kept behind the curtain by companies interested in maintaining the fiction of smart and autonomous machines.”14 And this is how we ourselves become enslaved to the archive.

The classical past does not merely inform the design and debates about artificial intelligence by way of mythic analogies. It forces us to confront the human infrastructure of intelligence itself. If we persist in the illusion of artificial intelligence free from human labor, we risk becoming permanently bowed at the altar of artificial gods.
